title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E449 develops power residues modulo a prime from the fact that the nonzero residues form a cyclic structure. On the previous page Euler argues as follows. Let P = 3n+1 be prime and let f, g, h < P be distinct with f^3 ≡ g^3 ≡ h^3 (mod P). Since g^3 − f^3 = (g−f)(f^2+fg+g^2) and P does not divide g−f, P divides f^2+fg+g^2, and likewise for the other two pairs. Differences of these give (h−g)(f+g+h), so P | f+g+h. Further combinations give P | f^2 − gh, P | fg+fh+gh and P | f^2+g^2+h^2.

This page completes Theorem 74: the three formulas f+g+h, fg+fh+gh and f^2+g^2+h^2 are each divisible by P. In modern terms f, g, h ≡ f, fω, fω^2 with ω a primitive cube root of unity mod P. So the elementary symmetric functions e1 and e2 vanish mod P, and x^3 − f^3 ≡ (x−f)(x−g)(x−h). The power sum p2 = e1^2 − 2e2 also vanishes.

Corollary 75 checks the case P = 19:
- 4^3 = 64 = 3·19 + 7, 6^3 = 216 = 11·19 + 7, and 9^3 = 729 = 38·19 + 7, so all three cubes leave residue 7.
- 4+6+9 = 19.
- 24+36+54 = 114 = 6·19.
- 16+36+81 = 133 = 7·19.

Theorem 76 has two parts. First, for every prime P ≡ 1 (mod 3) there exist numbers p^2+3q^2 divisible by P (implicitly with P not dividing p or q). Second, no number p^2+3q^2 is divisible by a prime ≡ 2 (mod 3) (implicitly with p, q not both divisible by it).

The proof of the first part takes two cubes with the same residue, so that P | f^2+fg+g^2. It then rewrites this binary form as p^2+3q^2 according to parity:
- if g is even: (f+g/2)^2 + 3(g/2)^2;
- if f is even: (f/2+g)^2 + 3(f/2)^2;
- if both are odd: ((f−g)/2)^2 + 3((f+g)/2)^2.
All three identities are correct.

The second part is begun at the bottom of the page and finished on the next. For P ≡ 2 (mod 3) cubing is a bijection on residues, so no difference g^3 − f^3 with 0 < f < g < P is divisible by P. Hence no f^2+fg+g^2 is divisible by P, and hence (Euler asserts) no p^2+3q^2 is either.

The purpose, completed in Corollaries 77–79 on the next page, is to determine the quadratic character of −3, and with it of +3, modulo every prime: −3 is a quadratic residue iff P ≡ 1 (mod 3). This is the supplementary-law case of quadratic reciprocity for −3, obtained here via cube roots of unity, since (2ω+1)^2 = −3.
errors: Theorem 76, second part, is stated without the necessary restriction: p^2+3q^2 is of course divisible by a prime ℓ ≡ 2 mod 3 when ℓ | p and ℓ | q. The intended statement needs p, q coprime to ℓ (or at least not both divisible by ℓ).

Logical gap in the second part. The parity identities only show that every f^2+fg+g^2 is of the form p^2+3q^2, which is the direction needed for the first part. To exclude divisors ≡ 2 mod 3 of p^2+3q^2, Euler needs the converse: every p^2+3q^2 equals some f^2+fg+g^2 with ℓ not dividing f−g. This is easily supplied by f = p−q, g = 2q, since (p−q)^2 + 2q(p−q) + 4q^2 = p^2+3q^2. If ℓ | f−g then p ≡ 3q, which forces ℓ | q and ℓ | p. Euler's 'quod proinde etiam ... locum habet' on the next page passes over this step.
Minor: the statement of the first part should exclude the trivial case where P divides both p and q. Euler's construction does give f, g < P not both divisible by P, so this is implicit.

ideas.what: Three cube roots of the same residue mod a prime 3n+1 have vanishing elementary symmetric functions e1, e2 and vanishing power sum p2 (Theorem 74), with numerical check for P = 19.
ideas.modern_name: Factorisation x^3 − a ≡ (x−f)(x−fω)(x−fω^2) mod p; 1+ω+ω^2 ≡ 0 for a primitive cube root of unity ω
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Euler's and Lagrange's work on polynomial congruences; made standard by Gauss (Disquisitiones, 1801)
ideas.where_published: E449 itself (Novi Commentarii 18, 1774; Opera Omnia I.3)

ideas.what: Every prime p ≡ 1 mod 3 divides some f^2+fg+g^2 (hence some x^2+3y^2), obtained from a nontrivial cube root of unity mod p.
ideas.modern_name: Existence of a primitive cube root of unity mod p ⇔ p ≡ 1 mod 3; −3 is a QR mod p (first step towards Fermat's p = x^2+3y^2)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (earlier proofs in E272 and related papers of c. 1759–1763); Fermat stated the theorem
ideas.where_published: E272 (Supplementum quorundam theorematum arithmeticorum) and E449

ideas.what: Reduction of the Eisenstein-type form f^2+fg+g^2 to p^2+3q^2 by parity case analysis.
ideas.modern_name: Equivalence of the forms x^2+xy+y^2 and x^2+3y^2 on representations (an index-2 sublattice relation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; systematised by Lagrange (1773–75) and Gauss
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on x^2+3y^2 (e.g. E272), E449

ideas.what: Primes 3n−1 divide no coprime p^2+3q^2, because cubing is a permutation of residues mod such a prime.
ideas.modern_name: −3 is a non-residue mod p ≡ 2 mod 3; cube map bijective when gcd(3, p−1) = 1

deep.surprise_reason: Theorem 74 is a pleasant elementary observation (symmetric functions of the three cube roots vanish mod p), but it is immediate from 1+ω+ω^2 ≡ 0. Theorem 76 is Euler's known treatment of the quadratic character of −3 via cube roots of unity, in a paper well represented in the Opera Omnia and in the standard histories (Weil). Nothing here appears absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially accurate. The radicals in the image are rendered as h in the transcription (the printed italic h looks like b in the scan); f, g, h is correct.
In the proof, the first identity in the image is (f + ½g)^2 + 3(½g)^2, matching the transcription.
